subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF HIGHER SALARIED EMPLOYEES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the annual report of the Public Service Commission released yesterday showed that the number of federal public servants has significantly risen in the past year. There are now four times the number of government employees earning over $50,000 than there were in 1981, and double the number earning between $40,000 and $50,000. This growth has been condoned by the government for its own questionable purposes at a time when it has been strongly urging everyone else to practise restraint. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson):
That the government launch an immediate investigation into why such growth at the high salaried level of the public service was allowed and promise that, when he is finished his work in Washington, Arthur Erickson not be hired to come to Ottawa and begin designing new, palatial government buildings to house this increasingly affluent multitude.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT HOUSE CONGRATULATE CANADA COUNCIL ON ITS WORK-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 25 years ago Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent tabled in Parliament a bill for the establishment of a Canada Council for the arts, humanities and social sciences, which received royal assent on March 28, 1957. On April 30 of that year, the first meeting of the Canada Council was held in the prime minister's own office.
Considering the tremendous development of Canadian artistic expression in subsequent years, for which the Canada Council is largely responsible, I move, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 and seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the House congratulate the Canada Council on its magnificent performance past and present, and that the House offer its best wishes for the continuation of the Council's success in the future.

subsubtopic: LABELLING OF CHEMICALS AND SPRAYS USED IN AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 on a very important matter with regard to the welfare of farmers. Metric conversion has caused a great deal of confusion to Canadians, but particularly to farmers. The farmers are beginning their planting season and are handling chemicals and sprays which are very important to the outcome of the crop but which could be hazardous to the well-being of the farmers if not properly handled. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That this House ask the government to place on the labelling of chemicals and sprays instructions requiring amounts in imperial measurements.

subsubtopic: OUTCOME OF HELSINKI GAMES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday afternoon in Helsinki the Soviet and Czech hockey teams played to a zero-zero tie, thereby depriving Canada of a deserved silver medal. It was obvious to most observers that neither team was trying to win, which would either have cost the Czechs the silver medal or the Soviets their unbeaten record. In other words, the fix was in. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That this House express its deep disappointment with the hockey federations of both the Soviet Union and Czechoslovakia for this unsportsmanlike display and that we call upon the International Ice Hockey Federation to change the play-off structure so that such a mockery cannot happen again.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: CANADA HOME RENOVATION PLAN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The minister is in the process of announcing-whether he has announced or not it is hard to say, it leaks out-a program called the Canada Home Renovation Plan. It is a program that perhaps will do something for our ailing construction industry, but is as yet just another plan with another series of initials, managed by his department. Could the minister advise the House whether the plan will be available to people generally across Canada? Will people be able in fact to borrow up to one third of the cost of renovations, provided it is within the ceiling of $3,000, for work done on their homes? Could the minister enlighten us with regard to the plan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: CANADA HOME RENOVATION PLAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the opportunity of talking about the plan. I could not, in the time allocated in question period, give all of the details. The hon. member

April 30, 1982
Oral Questions
indeed has touched on the main elements of the plan. The top limit is $3,000, available to each successful applicant.
The program will be available through the CMHC office in those areas where unemployment in the trade is most severe. I would invite hon. members to check with their own offices to see whether an allocation has been made in those areas. That will assist them in responding to people who probably will contact their offices, as some indeed have contacted my local constituency office this morning. It is a program involving $30 million, distributed across the country, to generate employment in the construction trades. It requires an individual participating to spend $2 for $1 of the grant, which is forgivable and non-taxable.

subsubtopic: CANADA HOME RENOVATION PLAN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, is the minister telling us that this is available only to selected Canadians in selected areas, and that the brochure produced by the minister-which says nothing about designated areas and represents that the plan is generally available to all Canadians-is in fact a plan available only to those Canadians who happen to live in those areas of Canada that the minister wants to favour?
Oh, oh!

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Madam Speaker, when the plan was announced approximatively a month ago, it was done in conjunction with the announcement of two other initiatives of the government directed especially to those areas in which there was high unemployment in the construction trades. I do not dispute the position of my hon. friend. This program is an additional $30 million directed to generate employment. It is directed specifically to those areas where that type of employment is in most serious difficulty.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING APPLICATION TO DESIGNATED AREAS
QUERY RESPECTING APPLICATION TO DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in view of the fact that there is tremendous unemployment in the building industry generally across the country, and in view of the fact that the materials for the building industry are almost all Canadian, why is the minister penalizing certain people, giving advantage to other people? Will the minister tell us if his riding of Scarborough is a designated area, and if Mississauga is a designated area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING APPLICATION TO DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the program for this additional $30 million was announced in conjunction with two other announcements at the same time. The first was an increase of 30,000 units
available this year under the Canada Rental Supply Plan. That plan is available across the country and is directed to those areas where there are low vacancy rates. We believe that that plan will generate at least an additional 60,000 man-years of employment in the construction trades.
Secondly, it was announced in conjunction with a change in the CHIP program, the home insulation program, where eligible home dwellings date from 1961 to 1971.
The combination of the three programs, Madam Speaker, was designed to assist those trades in the construction industry. We think that the combination of these plans across the country generally will have the beneficial effect of providing an incentive of jobs, at least an additional 100,000 jobs across the country. I cannot answer the specifics of the last part of the question.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PLAN COVER HOMES INSULATED WITH UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM
REQUEST THAT PLAN COVER HOMES INSULATED WITH UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with your permission I would direct a question to the same minister. The new Canada Home Renovation Plan, CHRP, does not apply to those thousands of Canadian homes which contain urea formaldehyde foam insulation. The government's so-called generous UFF1 plan, which the minister announced not too long ago, covers only about 5 per cent of homes with UFFI, leaving thousands of other houses with this insulation absolutely valueless because nobody wants to buy them. Why does the minister not apply the Canada Home Renovation Plan to those wishing to remove the foam, thereby creating jobs-that is the sole motivating drive for this aid plan-and help solve a major Canadian problem at the same time?
Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs): Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member should realize that the program we are offering home owners who insulated their homes with UFFI is actually far more generous than the other program to which he is referring here in the House.
The program for owners of homes insulated with UFFI provides for grants of up to $5,000, which are tax-free. The other program offers to pay up to 30 per cent of the cost of repairs, up to a maximum amount of $3,000. Therefore, it should be obvious to the hon. member that our program is the more generous of the two, because the amount offered may be as much as $5,000 and does not pay just a portion, but all of the repair costs involved.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the interesting thing about that plan is that it applies to only 5 per cent of the
April 30, 1982

homes which have urea formaldehyde foam insulation in them. The minister knows that, and his statement is misleading.

Madam Speaker, I want to ask a final supplementary question of the minister responsible for CMHC. The minister said today the grant is non-taxable. Is the minister now saying to the people of Canada that he is providing grants to households earning up to $48,000, tax free?	*

subtopic: ALSANDS PROJECT-GUARANTEES OFFERED TO PARTICIPATING COMPANIES
ALSANDS PROJECT-GUARANTEES OFFERED TO PARTICIPATING COMPANIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question, directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, concerns the Alsands project. In its attempt to bribe Gulf and Shell to maintain their position as partners, the government is offering to these advocates of competitive free enterprise a guaranteed market, guaranteed price, guaranteed financing and, finally, a guaranteed profit of 20 per cent. Where is the risk in this package for these companies which really believe in the spirit of competition? Where is the enterprise?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ALSANDS PROJECT-GUARANTEES OFFERED TO PARTICIPATING COMPANIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party is right in pointing out that the Government of Alberta and the Government of Canada together have put forward a very attractive proposal to the private sector, but I want to remind him, on the other hand, that he is wrong in some of the points he has made. First, there is no guaranteed price in this offer. Second, there is no guaranteed return in this offer either, since there is no guaranteed price.
The hon. member asked what the risks are. Obviously the risks are mainly in terms of being able to build a plant on time which would produce the quantity of oil it is planned to produce. The experience with the two existing plants, Suncor
Oral Questions
and Syncrude, has demonstrated that those plants are having some difficulties regularly in terms of production and that all the technological problems have not yet been solved, although many of them have. There are risks involved, and they are not insignificant.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT ENERGY PROJECTS BE MADE PUBLIC ENTERPRISES
REQUEST THAT ENERGY PROJECTS BE MADE PUBLIC ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the home owners who are losing homes all across Canada would like to have the so-called risks that the oil companies are being offered by the government in this deal, I can tell you. I stand by my earlier question.
Considering the whole range of concessions that the government has offered, particularly when it comes to financing, including the fact that the government is getting only 50 per cent of the equity and is putting up 85 per cent of the financing, why does the government not do what the vast majority of Canadians think is desirable, namely, that we should really be operating energy resources as public utilities and not as profit maximizing entities? Why does the Government of Canada not be courageous and straightforward when it comes to putting up this kind of money and, jointly with the Government of Alberta, make them into public enterprises?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: REQUEST THAT ENERGY PROJECTS BE MADE PUBLIC ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to remind the Leader of the New Democratic Party again that under this proposal there is no guaranteed price. If the price of oil were to decline or not increase as much as inflation, for instance, over the next ten to 20 years, the rate of return to the industry would be much lower than the one that is otherwise anticipated. There is a significant risk involved there. On the other hand, if there is a profit to be made, if there are significant benefits to be gained, then my hon. friend has partly answered the question himself by pointing out that the governments are equity participants for 50 per cent of the deal.
The people of Canada and the people of Alberta are going to benefit from the project in terms of return on their investment, not only in terms of getting oil. The Governments of Alberta and of Canada, contrary to the position of the New Democratic Party, still believe that it is better to have joint public-private partnership in this regard. We do not believe that the economy of Canada is necessarily going to be better just because it is run by the government, as the NDP would like us to do.

REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT HAVE HIGHER SHARE OF EQUITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister knows very well that the people of Canada, as taxpayers, are putting up a disproportionate amount of money and they are not getting equity for that. The multinational companies are once again taking the Liberal government to the

April 30, 1982

cleaners and holding the Government of Canada up to blackmail, and the government is backing down. I repeat, if we are putting up the dollars for risk investment in the energy sector, surely the Government of Canada should be saying that the people of Canada ought to get equity for every cent they put up. I ask the minister why this is not so.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

Madam Speaker, under this offer, Canadians will receive profits in proportion to their investments, if any profits are made. We shall have a 50 per cent equity in the project, and we shall be getting 50 per cent of any profits, in addition to the taxes, royalties, etc., that will be paid by the private sector partners in this specific project.
The hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party believes that the offer made by both governments was too generous. If, for some reason, participants in the consortium were to announce this afternoon that they were not going ahead with the project, I am sure the hon. member would rise in the House and accuse us of not having been generous enough.

subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING PROPOSAL TO COLLECT TAX FROM FISHERMEN AT SOURCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue and concerns the announcement made by the Minister of Finance in the November budget regarding the mandatory income tax deduction at source for fishermen. Does the government still plan to implement this policy, and when is it going to announce to the fishermen what percentage it will take from them when they land their catch at the buyer's wharf?

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING PROPOSAL TO COLLECT TAX FROM FISHERMEN AT SOURCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for this question. First of all there is no deduction at source in 1982. No requirement for that has gone out from the department because we have no legal authority until such time as the act is amended.

subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING PROPOSAL TO COLLECT TAX FROM FISHERMEN AT SOURCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING PROPOSAL TO COLLECT TAX FROM FISHERMEN AT SOURCE
speechtext: Allan MacEachen doesn't think so.

subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING PROPOSAL TO COLLECT TAX FROM FISHERMEN AT SOURCE
speechtext:
What the Minister of Finance did in a very responsive and responsible way, Madam Speaker, was to accede to the request of myself and other members of Parliament, and indeed fishermen and of at least one fishermen's union, to provide the legal authority for deducting fishermen's taxes at source. How that authority is administered is up to my department, and we are in the process of deciding how that is to be done.
I might say that on Wednesday morning the Atlantic Liberal caucus had a full discussion on this matter, some eminently reasonable suggestions were put forward, we are looking at them, and my department will announce shortly how we intend to administer the law after 1982. I can assure the hon. member and the fishermen that it will be administered in the best interests of the fishermen.

subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING PROPOSAL TO COLLECT TAX FROM FISHERMEN AT SOURCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am really glad to hear that it is not going ahead in 1982. However, my question would be: does this apply to the freshwater and west coast fishermen as well?

speechtext:
Bill S-19 is an important bill in terms of the ability of Canadians to recover damages and compensation from representatives in Canada of foreign governments, but I just want to point out that, according to my recollection, this is the first bill which has come out of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs by way of report since this session began. I do not want to be irrelevant, but I think it is relevant that there has been no priority given by this government to matters respecting justice and legal affairs. These matters are of secondary importance. I think it is fair to say-and I make no reflection-that the minds of government members are on other matters, and amendments to the Criminal Code dealing with the rights of Canadians to pursue legitimate claims against defendants are secondary in importance.
We hear much about this government's lack of commitment with respect to economic matters. I say that applies equally to matters of justice and legal affairs, the liberties and rights of Canadians to have their rights protected as they should be.
This is the first bill to come out of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I congratulate the government for this great victory; we now have before us Bill S-19 dealing
April 30, 1982

with diplomatic immunity. This is the extent of the government's accomplishment in the area of the rights of Canadians, and I suppose we should all be grateful. This weekend we will all go home feeling a glow of pride in our hearts because the government has moved so dramatically in the important area of protecting the rights of Canadians! I intend to go back to my constituents in Saskatoon West and tell them how proud I am of this government!
What other things are being dragged out in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs because of lack of commitment on the part of this government? My colleague, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), very appropriately pointed out today in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs that with respect to Bill C-43, which has been dealt with by the committee and almost completed, we now see the sad spectacle of this government's retreating from its commitment to freedom of information. The government very rightly is subject to the serious criticism of public opinion across the country. The government has no commitment to freedom of information and no commitment to civil liberties. The only commitment of the government is to make sure the people of Canada can sue, in certain limited circumstances, foreign diplomats in cases of civil liability. What a great record this government has! I think it should be commended. I say that, of course, without any seriousness at all.
What about Bill C-61, the proposed Young Offenders Act? We dealt with that expeditiously. Why is that not on the floor of the Elouse of Commons to be dealt with?

subsubtopic: IMMUNITY OF FOREIGN STATES IN CANADIAN COURTS
speechtext:
Bill S-19 is before us, and we say Bill S-19 is a light at the end of the tunnel. After a great deal of effort on the part of the official opposition to put pressure on the government to take action, it has finaly moved.
If one looks at Bill S-19, one might get the impression from the title that it is a bill which extends diplomatic immunity to representatives of foreign countries operating in Canada. However, that is not the case; quite the contrary. It is an attempt to codify and set forth in statutory form the provisions, rights and limitations on diplomatic immunity, the rights of foreign countries to carry on so-called commercial activities in our country and the extent to which they are going to be held responsible with respect to contracts, loss, liability or damages suffered by Canadian citizens in the course of carrying on that commercial activity. There is an attempt here to specify the limitations placed on foreign countries represented in Canada and their agents.

I was in my riding when an election was called for April 26. In my riding the result was unanimous, though I take no personal pride in that and no responsibility for it; I just happened to be there doing the government's work, carrying out my responsibilities as a member of Parliament. I admit that I was not here regularly in the last two weeks, but I believe that my constituents desire personal attention occasionally and so I go to my riding to help them. If an election should happen to coincide, that is something over which I have no control.
I have been diverted, Mr. Speaker, when I have been trying to deal with this important legislation and rush it through the House on a Friday afternoon. As we know, this important legislation has to be dealt with, as has the government's record of commitment to civil liberties and the ability of Canadians to protect their interests in the courts of our land.
In the world today there are many governments-including our own-which are getting involved in what are called centrally controlled economies. This involves the creation of so-called Crown corporations. It is an involvement by government in commercial activity which normally has been confined to the area of private endeavour. This legislation is important in that it gives us an opportunity to review circumstances where we have not only the normal diplomatic representation in our country and the normal immunity that is given to such representatives-which is right and proper-but we are facing a situation where governments, agencies of governments and representatives of governments have become involved in commercial endeavours.
Petro-Canada is an example, for which representatives of the People's Republic of China are doing some work on the

April 30, 1982
State Immunity Act
offshore. We also have representatives of Canadian commercial enterprises in other countries, and, of course, other countries have representatives in this country who deal commercially with private citizens and with corporations.
In terms of international law it is important for us to review the rights that Canadians have vis-a-vis representatives of foreign governments, whether they be diplomatic representatives or representatives of agencies that carry on commercial activities. We must consider the right of Canadians to collect compensation for wrongful acts.
The legislation was considered in committee and some concerns were expressed in the course of those hearings. I commend the parliamentary secretary for his conduct of the legislation through the committee. It is too bad that the Minister of Justice was not available at that time but the parliamentary secretary is one Liberal who attended committee.
There is a story going around the Hill that the Minister of Justice has been seen at the Standing Committee of Justice and Legal Affairs. I have not had that story confirmed but I am prepared to put the resources of the research staff of this party to work this weekend to see whether it can be verified.

subsubtopic: IMMUNITY OF FOREIGN STATES IN CANADIAN COURTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will deal expeditiously with this legislation if I can get the attention of hon. members on the Liberal side, who insist on trying to interrupt a serious discussion. If I could get their attention I would point out some of the concerns that have been expressed by this party and by witnesses before the committee about the vagueness of the term "commercial activity" which appears in the bill. As presently defined, it means "any particular transaction, act or conduct or any regular course of conduct that by reason of its nature is of a commercial character".
To me that sounds like a definition that commercial activity means commercial activity. It does not elaborate on what kind of activity will be covered by legislation in this country and that would allow individual citizens to pursue to their remedy.
The British law in this area is far more specific. It enumerates the three headings that are included in the term "commercial transaction" as follows:
1)	any contract for supply of goods or services
2)	any loan or other transaction for the provision of finance and any guarantee or indemnity in respect of any such transaction or of any other financial obligation; and
3)	any other transaction or activity (whether of a commercial, industrial, financial, professional or other similar character) into which a state enters or in which it engages otherwise than in the exercise of sovereign authority.
The British law is specific and indicates to the litigant interested in pursuing his or her rights the areas in which this may be done. In this country it will be necessary to develop a body of jurisprudence through the courts. The courts will have the opportunity to define the term "commercial activity" and specify what activities will be available for legal recourse and what activities will not.
A witness who came before the committee, Mr. J. M. Robinson, a lawyer who works in the area of lending to foreign sovereign countries, was most concerned that these arrangements for lending would be protected by the bill, particularly in light of the Polish and now the Argentine monetary crisis. Officials of the department assured us, on the basis of their legal advice, that the situation would be covered. They also assured us that it would be better to leave the definition as broad as possible. Their point of view was that by using very specific definitions, the range of applicability of a section narrows.
I am not totally satisfied with their response, but I am prepared to let this bill go through. I know the Department of Justice will monitor the situation to make sure that the definition is reasonably broad and that we will not be restricting the rights of Canadians vis-a-vis foreign representatives. I would have preferred the other system of definition for more precision and guidance to the courts, and the litigants themselves would have had a better idea of their rights under the legislation.
When I spoke on second reading of this bill I indicated my concerns with respect to enforcement, by execution or otherwise, of civil judgments. Remedies under this legislation are still restricted. Specific performance, injunctive relief, and an order for recovery of land unless the foreign state itself consents, are not available.
I understand the official's argument that these remedies are not available against the Crown in Canada. On the basis of some activities which have been taking place on behalf of Crown corporations in the courts of this land, I think it is fair to say that any commercial enterprise operated by the Government of Canada now apparently has the right to claim immunity from prosecution, and that puts the government in a very strong position. We can see that it is difficult to expect that Canadians will be able to collect against agents of foreign governments when criminal prosecution of government agencies, Crown corporations and ministers is virtually impossible, at least on the basis of the ruling in the uranium cartel case. However, I think that is an area which we must continue to monitor because of the fact that foreign governments are involved through state agencies, whether it be the Soviet Union or countries in the free world. There has been a movement toward centrally controlled economies and commercial activities through government agencies, and I think those agencies should do business in Canada according to the rules that apply to every other citizen of Canada. I think we should keep an eye

on the situation with a view to bringing in amendments to this legislation if there has been any serious abuse.
I said I would be brief, Mr. Speaker, and I have been. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to impose unduly on the House this afternoon in discussing the provisions of Bill S-19. There are, however, a couple of matters which I think deserve mention, even if the time has passed for introducing appropriate amendments to bridge a gap between this particular bill and an act which is now on the statute books.
Obviously, Bill S-19 has been brought forward-although it is slightly misnamed, if I might say so-because of the growth of state enterprises of one kind or another operating both

April 30, 1982
State Immunity Act
domestically and abroad. We all know about Crown enterprises in this country. We do not know how many of them we have as Crown corporations; I gather that figure is still in dispute. A good many operate in Canada, but that should not worry law makers except that we do not know how many Crown corporations there are.
This bill is directed toward state enterprises overseas and their operations in this country, particularly when they are involved in a commercial enterprise of one kind or another. The normal function of a state, the traditional, historic function when it is operating abroad, made it possible for receiving states to accord immunity to the operations of a sending state when it had a representative in the country. This, of course, was the origin of diplomatic immunity. Clause 3 of the bill provides:
Except as provided by this Act, a foreign state is immune from the jurisdiction of any court in Canada.
We remember the old saying "Don't shoot the messenger". If a messenger brought a message from a foreign state that the foreign state is at war with the receiving state, we would hear: "Don't shoot the messenger; look to someone else to attack". This, in very simple form, is the origin of diplomatic immunity.
There is another act on the statute books, Chapter 31 of the Statutes of Canada, 1976-1977, which gives substance in law to the Vienna convention on diplomatic relations. There we find what the standard functions of a diplomatic mission are. If we were dealing only with diplomatic missions, it would be simple. But because of the growth of state activities beyond their diplomatic activities in foreign countries, a bill such as S-19 was required.
Article 3 of the Vienna convention, which is a schedule to the Diplomatic and Consular Privileges and Immunities Act which I have already cited as Chapter 31 of the Statutes of Canada 1976-77, provides that:
The functions of a diplomatic mission consist inter alia in: (a) representing the sending State in the receiving State; (b) protecting in the receiving State the interests of the sending State and of its nationals, within the limits permitted by international law; (c) negotiating with the Government of the receiving State: (d) ascertaining by all lawful means conditions and developments in the receiving State, and reporting thereon to the Government of the sending State: (e) promoting friendly relations between the sending State and the receiving State, and developing their economic, cultural and scientific relations.
Those are standard diplomatic functions. Generally speaking, in the performance and execution of the duties related to those functions there is traditionally an immunity accorded to the agents of the sending state in the receiving state. When the sending state embarks on activities beyond the diplomatic and becomes involved in matters of commercial enterprise- whether selling grain, oil, buying Candus or grain-this bill makes it clear that the foreign state is not immune from the jurisdiction of a court in any proceedings that relate to "-any damage to or loss of property that occurs in Canada". This would also be true in the area of shipping or transporting material. I suspect that one of the reasons this bill is before us is that there was a state-owned ship which managed to leave
behind it in a Canadian port a mountain of debt which the host company had to assume, with no recourse against the offending state to collect damages. I think that this state immunity bill has been introduced for this and other reasons. As I said, Clause 6(b) of this bill makes it clear that the foreign state is not immune from the jurisdiction of a court in any proceedings relating to damage or loss of property that occurs in Canada.
This brings me to the core of the problem I would like to address. Up until now the statute on the books has dealt with state organisms, not individuals. I feel there must be some protection for individual Canadians. I merely say this because I believe it is important to know that damages suffered by Canadian citizens who enter into contracts in good faith with foreign government agents, particularly in rental situations, and who discover at the termination of the lease that they can be left with a large number of bills for the restoration of damaged leased property, are not taken into account in this Bill. It has happened to me and many others on more than one occasion. There are individuals who are being missed by these two pieces of legislation. There should be some way to protect individual Canadians, either through this bill or the act, from damage which might occur to the property which they rent in good faith to the representative of a foreign state.
I noted in this bill that the foreign state is not immune, but we seem to be missing the individual in this legislation. I hope that the government could at least introduce some small piece of legislation which would take into account what may occur to individuals.
Article 30 of the privileges and immunities convention states that:
The private residence of a diplomatic agent-
Presumably that is a diplomatic officer who has been sent to any foreign country:
-shall enjoy the inviolability and protection of the premises of the mission.
If we return to Article 22 of the convention, we find that:
The premises of the mission shall be inviolable.
Presumably because of that inviolability, the immunity is extended to the premises occupied by a diplomatic agent living abroad. This is an instance where Canadians can suffer. I believe there is a case before the courts-I do not know its status-concerning an individual who rented a premises to a foreign state. For reasons unknown to me, the premises were vacated in mid-winter, without notice, and the pipes froze. A great deal of damage was done to this property and when the owner discovered that the pipes were broken after his tenants had left, he tried to get redress through the courts for the losses he incurred in restoring his house to its proper state. The courts found that the state which had leased the property could claim immunity. This immunity applies even when a diplomatic agent is renting the property, because it is usually the state which signs the lease on behalf of that agent, thereby allowing it to claim immunity from any damages which might occur to that property.
Therefore, I believe that neither Bill S-19 or Chapter 31 of the Statutes of Canada, 1976-77, really extend to individual
April 30, 1982

Canadians the protection they need when dealing with foreign powers.
I merely put this on the record now and urge that this gap be closed. I am sure that it is in the interest of this Parliament to realize that one of its duties is to protect Canadian citizens.
I found it strange to learn this morning that one of the inverted pieces of logic in Bill S-19 is that foreign commercial enterprises operating in Canada have their immunity removed but Canadian Crown corporations are still able to claim immunity. That is an anomaly which this particular bill does not address and does nothing to remove.
A second anomaly which I would like to point out is that not only are individual Canadians inadequately protected from the activities of a foreign state, but they are also not protected from the activities of a Crown corporation in their own country, against whom they will have the greatest difficulty to bring suit.
Elaving put those two matters on the record, I close and thank the House for its indulgence.

speechtext:
that the bill be read the third time and do pass.
Mr. Speaker, a year ago 1 thought this bill would be passed quickly, and that was mainly because of the fact that Bill C-58 was almost identical to Bill C-21, tabled on November 5, 1979 by the Progressive Conservative Party in power at the time, and more specifically, by the hon. member for Nepean-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker). In addition, as early as in 1976, the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections had recommended shortening the election period. In 1975, the Chief Electoral Officer submitted a report under the title, "An Examination of Possible Ways of Reducing the Election Period." In his report, the Chief Electoral Officer made a thorough study of perma-
Canada Elections Act
nent lists and continuous voter files. He estimated at the time that it would cost about $30 million per year to maintain a voter filing system that could be updated on a continuing basis up to the time an election was held.
After weighing the pros and cons of permanent voter lists, the Chief Electoral Officer found that it would be possible to substantially shorten the election period by eliminating the printing of preliminary lists and their distribution to voters to inform them that their names were on the list. Early in 1976, the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections discussed the report by the Chief Electoral Officer at several meetings. It became clear that committee members did not, at the time, find it desirable to introduce a permanent list or a continuous voter file. The committee did, however, announce that it was in favour of shortening the election period by eliminating the printing of preliminary lists. On March 23, 1976, it passed a motion to that effect.

So, Mr. Speaker, it is plain to see that support for the two major changes proposed by this bill has a fairly long history. Furthermore, we have taken into account some members' fears that we might be shortening the election period too much, especially in parts of the country where communication and travel are difficult. As a result, we proposed an amendment to the bill, at Clause 2, to change the latest day on which the writ of an election would be issued, from the forty-seventh day to the fiftieth day before polling day. This change was received positively by the Conservative members on the standing committee when it was presented by my parliamentary secretary, and it appears in the amended version of the bill we now have before us.
The second change in Bill C-58 which was brought about in the standing committee concerns the length of the period for enumeration. In the original version of Bill C-58, enumeration was to begin on the thirty-fifth day before polling day and end on the thirty-second day. In other words, enumeration was to take place during a four-day period. Members on both sides of the committee expressed reservations about having only four days for enumeration. The government, after listening to their views on this matter, agreed to change the bill.
Since the first change to the bill which I have just described added three days to the minimum election period, it was a simple matter to add three more days to the enumeration period without disturbing the dates for carrying out the other activities that are required for the preparation and conduct of an election. This change in the enumeration period required amendments to the text of the bill in several places, namely, Clauses 3, 5, 6 and 7. All these minor changes in wording were approved unanimously by the standing committee.
I feel that this new seven-day minimum period for enumeration is an improvement over the present practice, which allows six days for enumeration to be carried out. As a result of these amendments, we can feel confident that there will be enough

April 30, 1982
Canada Elections Act
time for the enumerators to do as thorough a job as possible. I believe we owe this to all Canadians, who expect that we should make it as easy as possible for them to exercise their democratic franchise.
Much credit must be given to the standing committee members for their role in coming to agreement on this bill and for improving its text. All members of Parliament and Canadians in general should be grateful for their thorough review of the text of Bill C-58.
In closing, I should like to express my gratitude, and that of all members, to the Chief Electoral Officer, Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel, and his staff. Their very professional and courteous assistance played an important role in helping members of the committee understand and improve the text of this bill.
Finally, I would express my personal wish that after eight hours of debate at second reading and six meetings of the standing committee, we could complete our study of this bill very shortly. The committee members looked at the bill in detail and all parties agreed to the amendments that were put. I see no reason for much more discussion of Bill C-58, and I hope that my friends opposide will allow its passage before four o'clock today.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to listen to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), one would think he has just presented us with the Declaration of Independence or some other very important piece of legislation. I would remind you Honour that what the bill does, as has been mentioned, is to change two very minor things. It shortens an election writ period by a few days and it increases the enumeration period by a few days. Considered in the light of the problems we have with parliamentary and representative democracy in Canada, I hope to show that it is an awfully small piece of legislation. It has been overworked. It is similar to the idea of using a band-aid for appendicitis. However, speaking for my part of Canada, western Canada, this bill will not make anyone happier about our federal institutions. It will make some of them unhappy.
Concerning the first point I want to make, I stress that I am speaking only for myself and not for the party at all. My first point concerns the question of rural ridings. Your Honour is from a suburban riding. I assure your Honour that you cannot imagine, nor can any of us who are from urban ridings, the problem involved in rural ridings in getting people to come out for nomination meetings, perhaps from several communities. There are problems involved in getting ads into newspapers which are published weekly, perhaps on a monthly basis in some cases. There are problems involved in travelling around ridings to visit people. Parties have problems in trying to get candidates to come forward.
From my limited knowledge of the subject, it would appear that the reason we reduced the number of days for the writ period is that some people in central Canada, those in urban ridings, think election campaigns are too long. However, I can assure your Honour that, as I understand it, people in the rural
ridings across Canada, including those in your Honour's province, are in favour of longer campaigns.
I think many of these people would feel that a better title for the bill would be "an act to ensure the re-election of incumbents to the maximum feasible extent", and I am only being half facetious. To that extent, I would express disagreement with the unstated principle, which is to try to re-elect incumbents. We have enough advantages now as incumbents that I think reducing the election period would be just one more advantage, and would not necessarily ensure that the best people are elected to sit in this House. This is not a good principle on which to embark. Why not reduce the period to two weeks? I bet even the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) would be re-elected if we had a two-week election period.
Another problem with shortening the election period is that it is difficult for a public servant, and I am an example, to decide whether he wishes to run. It is also difficult for people in business. This may not apply to professionals, but for those in many occupations the longer the writ period, the better. The bill makes it harder for people such as federal public servants to run in an election. We will also be heading in the direction of denying ourselves the best people for public office.
My next point is to ask why two very small matters have been blown up into a bill. There have been all kinds of hearings and debate. At the same time we have ignored some of the major recommendations made by the Chief Electoral Officer, Jean-Marc Hamel, in the 1979 and 1980 elections.
I will give two examples. The first is the question of posting voters' lists on telephone poles in the ridings. I have just returned from Saskatchewan where voters' lists are posted on telephone poles in every community. For example, it lists Mary Smith, her address and the fact that she lives alone. It is outrageous that in urban communities where there is a lot of crime everyone should be advised that Mary Smith lives in a house on such and such a street in such and such a place. One of the recommendations of Mr. Hamel and of many women's groups is that this no longer be allowed. They recommend that each voter be sent a notice to show that he or she is on the voters' list. This information should not be posted. If it will prevent one woman from being raped or one widow from being mugged or having her house broken into, it is infinitely important that that be written into the bill. It should be done. In the very least such a meaningful amendment should be made to our Elections Act. I feel very strongly about this.
Coming from Quebec, Mr. Speaker, I do not think you could possibly appreciate my next point. Election results in most parts of eastern Canada are known to British Columbians when they go to vote. They know how the rest of the country in the different time zones has voted. We have moved into the electronic age and during an election, radio stations in Seattle broadcast information on how many Liberals have been
April 30, 1982

elected in Ontario and Quebec. People in Vancouver have full knowledge that the election has already been decided before they cast their votes.
This is why a number of people, including the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) and myself, have proposed a very simple process of juggling the hours. Maybe the people of Newfoundland would not have as many hours in which to vote. However, all votes will be counted at the same time. It would not inconvenience the people in your riding, Mr. Speaker, to wait an hour or two until the people in Vancouver were finished voting before the votes in the riding of Lachine were counted. From the standpoint of our institutions, I cannot stress too strongly that it creates all kinds of problems for our democracy when voters in large chunks of Canada know how voters in other parts of Canada have voted.
During the 1880s or 1890s, elections took place over a one or two-week period. That was the reason we moved to having elections all at the same time, hopefully at the same hour. But we forgot that we cannot control the electronic media outside Canada. I am not talking about someone in Ontario calling someone in British Columbia; it is the radio and television stations outside Canada that we cannot control. This is something else that should have been taken care of in this bill. Votes should not be counted in one part of Canada before being cast in another part. There are many other recommendations which should have been written into this bill.
I now want to deal with the question of redistribution. Coming from a province which is supposed to get additional seats under the new formula, naturally you, Mr. Speaker, are in favour of redistribution. I appreciate that no province will have less seats under the existing formula and that your province will get an additional four seats.
My point is that there are probably too many of us in this House now. I do not think we have to reduce the number of seats in any province; we are capable of coming up with a formula that ensures that no province loses any seats and that provinces which grow very quickly will have more seats.
Members may ask, what is my formula. I have not been able to come up with one. I do not think our caucus can accommodate me either. However, that is the direction in which we should be going. There should be a clause in the bill which contains a formula whereby no province shall lose any seats, but provinces which grow shall have the number of its seats increased. That would be a significant offer of hope to people in my region of Canada who know that they are vastly underrepresented in terms of our growing population.
It is no secret that the people of Canada have a lot of criticism respecting members of Parliament. They do not think we should add 28 members to this House at a cost of $140,000 each, including personal and staff salaries, as they do not believe Parliament is functioning properly at this moment. Partly on the basis of cost, and partly because we should come up with a formula to give us a few more seats without depriving any province of its present number of seats, I believe that point should have been dealt with in this bill.
I understand the President of the Privy Council sent letters to all elections commissions across Canada advising them to
Canada Elections Act
get on with the revision of the electoral boundaries to increase the representation by 28 seats. The problem is that the same thing may happen that happened in 1972 and 1974. The commissions came up with new boundaries and we looked at the maps which contained the new boundaries. I believe in about 1983 or 1984 there will be a suspension act saying that everything that has been done will be scrapped. I urge the government not to do that; it would not be healthy for this country. Once again, all this should have been included in Bill C-68.
That brings me to the question: What are our federal institutions doing at the moment, and how do Canadians look at them? For interest, Mr. Speaker, I did a survey in my own riding, a somewhat random survey, and you may be interested in some of the comments. One question was: "Do you favour continuing the existing size of the House of Commons?" In one sample 50 per cent said yes; in another sample, 53 per cent said yes. As to no, it was 13 per cent and 26 per cent. Obviously the majority of people who pay taxes in my riding do not want to see the House changed.
Another question related to another institution, the Supreme Court, was: "Do you consider that the Supreme Court of Canada tends to favour the federal or provincial government in its constitutional decisions?" In the answer one sample had 50 per cent favouring the federal government and another had 28 per cent. To the question as to how many favoured the provinces, I had two results. One was zero per cent and one was 1 per cent. There was a large number undecided.
Question 3 was: "Would you favour any change in the composition of the Supreme Court of Canada?" How many said yes? In one sample it was 47 per cent; in the other sample it was 55 per cent; the noes were 25 per cent and 11 per cent. Again, this only makes the point that a lot of people in my riding feel that the Supreme Court of Canada should become an institution in which we can all have more confidence.
Another question was: "Would you favour giving the provinces as a group a role in making, say, half the appointments to a restructured Supreme Court?" Listen to this. One sample: yes, 72 per cent; no, 14 per cent.
Coming to the Senate, the question was: "Do you think the present Senate should be altered?" The answer was: yes, one sample, 66 per cent; 9 per cent said no. In the other sample 85 per cent said yes, but only 6 per cent said no.
The next question was: "Do you think there is a meaningful role for any form of upper chamber in an updated Constitution?" The number who said yes in the first sample was 50 per cent, with 22 per cent saying no. In the second sample, for yes it was 61 per cent, and no, 29 per cent.
The next question may be an interesting one: "If yes, what basic model would you favour?" Elected: the answer was 47 per cent in the First sample, whereas 53 per cent said senators appointed by provincial governments only. In the second

April 30, 1982
Canada Elections Act
sample it was 58 per cent for an elected Senate and 36 per cent favouring the provinces to elect the Senate.
The next one-I think this should be put on the record-had regard to federal agencies. The question was: "Should the provincial governments as a group have a right to appoint, say, half the members of the board of the Bank of Canada, the CRTC, the CBC, the CTC, the NEB, etc?" In the first sample the yes response was 53 per cent and the no was 31 per cent. In the second sample the yes response was 65 per cent and the no was 26 per cent.
Another question: "Should our lieutenant governors be nominated by Ottawa as they are now?" Some 45 per cent said yes while 55 per cent said the provincial governments should appoint them.
The next question was: "Should our Queen's Bench judges be appointed in future by Ottawa as they are now?" The answer was, 42 per cent for Ottawa and 57 per cent for appointment by the provincial governments. I guess that is enough of that, Mr. Speaker.
What I am trying to say is that respect for institutions in Canada and I think the Gallup polls show it too-is not what you and 1 would like it to be, Mr. Speaker, though perhaps for different reasons. The institution that has the least respect, I suggest, is the Senate of Canada.
Someone once said of the House of Lords in Britain that the cure for admiring the House of Lords was to go and look at it. There is a quote from Walter Bagot:
The whole history of civilization is strewn with creeds and institutions which were invaluable at first, and deadly afterwards.
I took up the list of senators today, and I would respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that if you or any of our colleagues look over the list, it would be very interesting. Without getting into personalities, I would respectfully suggest that any former premier of a province should be entitled to be a senator. A mayor of a large city should be entitled also, under our present system, as should a member of a CRT, a trade union, an association or institution in the service sector, or a church. All of these, including university leaders, professors, professional people, should be entitled to be senators. But by any independent criteria such as that, considering a lot of our senators-and I exclude many of them because obviously some are doing good work and working hard-our Senate is not, to put it this way, acceptable in its present form to most Canadians.
What is the answer? I suggest an elected Senate. I have recently, over the last while, changed the view that it should be one appointed by the province, like the Bundesrat in West Germany. It should be an elected Senate with an equal number of senators from each province. That is perhaps the surest and best reform we can make of the parliamentary institution.
I understand that every federal system of government- someone will correct me if I am wrong-in the world has an upper chamber. I am convinced that our Senate could become a more meaningful and acceptable institution if it were elected. One can ask, should it be elected every time there is a general election, or should it be elected by rotations, with one-third
retiring every four years? I think any Canadian of goodwill is open to discussion on that. I wish that subject had been looked at by the committee which was considering the bill before us today. If we had eight senators from every provnce in Canada-I do not say for a moment that some of the present senators would not be in that group-we would have an institution that everybody in this House and in Canada could be proud of.
One might ask, what powers would you give them? Again, I do not have any firm views on that. Perhaps they should not be entitled to present money bills. We do know that our elected Senate is working in Australia, in the United States and in the Republic of Ireland. It is working in many places.
I find it interesting that Senator Roblin, a former premier of Manitoba, made a speech not long ago, in June, 1980, in which he called for an elected Senate. I think he accepted, as I read the notes here, that the Senate in its present form will not do. I should add that a number of senators seem to have accepted that as well. He pointed out that Bill C-60 of your government, Mr. Speaker, tried to introduce a House of the Federation. The Pepin-Robarts commission suggested a Council of the Federation. The Ryan report in Quebec wanted a federal council. The Canada West Foundation called for a House of the Provinces. The Canadian Bar Association and others had other ideas. He goes on to point out that the fact that none of these has proposed an elected Senate he considers to be an error, and I join in that view.
How could we not have a better Senate if it were elected? Senators would then have to go back to their electors and account for their acts. Senators could then do the excellent committee work they are doing now, but as elected men and women. As hon. members perhaps know, people in the west are seriously under-represented in the Senate in terms of population. Some might ask how we can give Prince Edward Island eight senators when there are only 120,000 people there, and how we could give Ontario only eight senators when there are eight million people in Ontario? There would be a million people per senator. However, I submit that the people in central Canada are sufficiently concerned-as are those of us who do not live in central Canada-about what is happening to our respect for parliamentary institutions that they would probably be the first to recommend an elected Senate. Eight senators from Quebec, for instance, would fight tooth and nail for the interests of Quebec. Eight senators from Prince Edward Island would also fight tooth and nail for Prince Edward Island. What person in this House would deny Prince Edward Island the opportunity to have eight senators? I do not think anyone of goodwill would.
It is too easy for a person to say that the trouble with the Senate is that the appointments have not been of premiers of provinces, that there have not been enough people of independent stature in their communities and that the answer is simply to appoint, for lack of a better word, more qualified people to
April 30, 1982

the Senate. However, in my submission it is too late for that. We cannot go back. We are in such a position now that we must go ahead and elect senators from all the regions of Canada. According to the poll, the people of my region of Canada would like that. I know many people in this chamber and in central Canada are concerned about the enormous antipathy building against the government, which is elected from two provinces. This would be one way of providing an outlet for western Canadians and, hopefully, for maritimers, Quebecers and Ontarians.
There are other institutions I could mention which are well beyond the bounds of this bill. I suppose I should not talk about courts and boards except to say that I believe strongly that we should give the provinces a chance to appoint, say, half the directors of the CBC and half the commissioners of CRTC, or at least give them a chance to confirm appointments such as one recently to the head of the CBC. Perhaps we could work out a system which would give members of Parliament a chance to have at least an advisory capacity or consent capacity in relation to these order in council appointments which, as hon. members know, take effect the minute they are signed.
1 remember a time when I was in court with another lawyer; at the lunch hour his appointment was signed and he could not continue with the case in the afternoon. Is that proper? Would it not be better that a lawyer should at least pass before a committee of the Senate or a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons before he is confirmed in the position?
I am told there are 650 federal judges in Canada. While perhaps a third of them are outstanding and a third satisfactory, in my view a third of the judges in superior courts in Canada should not be sitting in those courts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted you recognized me because I am hoping to get to a meeting with the government House leader shortly. If I had to wait for another turn, the meeting might not take place and perhaps no more business would ever be done! I want to take a moment or two to speak about the bill. I will not take more than ten minutes, but I think the bill is important enough that I make at least some comments.
The bill has received a great deal of consideration. Each and every caucus probably agonized over whether the reduction in the minimum election period is an appropriate reduction. I think the compromise worked out is acceptable, but I want to say, partly in answer to other people's comments and partly in answer to the thoughts of certain people across the country who may be interested in a matter such as the period for elections, that I do not really think it matters too much whether we reduce the election period to 50 days or not.
When I was in the legislative assembly in Ontario the period was 37 days. It seemed to me at the time to be an adequate length of time. The period for the recent Saskatchewan election was even shorter, but that did not inhibit the electors from making the choice to defeat a very large number of incumbents.
I suggest that sometimes we get wrapped up in the idea that the shorter the election period the easier it is for incumbents to be re-elected. I suppose theoretically-and even in practice- that could be true if we were to shorten the period so dramatically as to make it impossible for anyone else to get into the race, but I think anything in excess of a month and a half is probably long enough to allow any candidate or political party to represent individual or collective views adequately and in sufficient time for the people of the country who, in my personal judgment after 15 years in politics, pay much more attention to the platforms and the quality of candidates than we perhaps give them credit for. A month and a half does afford a sufficiently long period of time. This does not preclude in any way the kind of electioneering that goes on by people seeking office, whether they are incumbents or otherwise, for years on end. People can canvass door to door regardless of whether it is a year before, two years before or ten years before the election in which they intend to run, and they can become very, very well known. They can in fact get to the point where they can call almost everyone on every street in every constituency by name. The actual official period of time is probably of lesser importance than some of us who are more involved directly in politics might believe.
If there is a deficiency in the bill it is that it deals with a very narrow aspect of the elections, and if it had not come up for discussion for another year it would have made very little difference. I do not expect the changes in this legislation to alter dramatically the outcome of the next or of any other

It may be inappropriate but I would venture the opinion that if an election were held today or tomorrow we would find that the vast majority of Canadians had already made up their minds at least about who they are not going to vote for. I think the majority of people have decided "out with the Liberals". That is my personal view, and of course it may not be shared by everyone in the House.

speechtext:
The minister says he will wait for two years to find out. Although the majority of people would not agree with that, I cannot blame him. I do not think if I were in government I would want to test these policies at the ballot box any more than he would.
The changes proposed in this legislation are acceptable. The reduction in the length of time may make it easier for candidates to campaign. The changes made at committee in the enumeration period were certainly necessary. In some of the larger constituencies it is very difficult to get the enumeration done in four days. It is going to become more and more difficult to find people to do the enumeration. We just do not pay enough so that we can find people on short notice. And with the increase in two-parent-working families it is difficult to find people at home. Although seven days have been allotted, I dare say we will find that there are only three or at the most four hours per day when people can be found at home and have their eligibility to vote checked. That provision might even have to be reviewed before an election to see if the length of time is adequate.
Nomination day is set at 28 days before the election, and that is fine. Examining and sealing the ballot box in the returning office 21 days before the vote could be of value if it is used properly.
We have to look at the whole process, Mr. Speaker. Although the current process is unwieldly and cumbersome, that is not the problem now. The period of time involved in all the other attendant factors is not going to make for a better government or a better Parliament or a more responsible
representative process. The major changes must take place in the House. To afford people an opportunity to cast a ballot is the single most important part of the democratic process but after the ballot is cast and the election is over, the follow-up is the measure of the success of the process.
Regardless of what changes we make to the Canada Elections Act, unless we come to grips with the archaic system in which Parliament must work-and today was a good example of it-and deal with the relevance of any change to the election process, we will not have a better representative Parliament than we have now.
I do not think you were in the chair this morning Mr. Speaker. I listened to one hon. member debate a bill which came up for debate before this one. Without being uncharitable let me say that I could not help but feel that much of the 35 or 40 minutes was used up on extraneous matters and not on dealing with the content of the bill. This happens because the opportunity for members to gain the floor is limited and when they do, they speak for far too long. The tendency is to use up the time.
We must address ourselves to the question of follow-up. If these changes to the Canada Elections Act are to have any meaning we have to address ourselves to the changes in the day to day operations of the House of Commons and its committees. There is no purpose in going through this exercise today if we continue with the archaic system that does not allow for meaningful debate and gives little opportunity for a proper exchange of views. The present rules almost require members to speak twice as long as they need to, just to take up the time that is available to them. That is not to say that every time a member speaks for 40 minutes the time is wasted. Of course there are times when 20, 30 and 40-minute speeches are justified because of the content of the matter under discussion.
This bill is only a first step, Mr. Speaker. In fact, it may even be said to be the last step. I do not think the changes need to take place right away. The world will not change one iota because of this series of amendments. Indeed, it might have been better had we taken on first the chore of reforming the parliamentary process and, by showing the public that Parliament can work, in that way encouraged its participation. We must encourage people to feel that casting a ballot is an important function in a democratic process. They must feel that when they send someone to Parliament that person has an opportunity to express the views of the constituents and put forward different point of view about how the country should evolve.
I will stop at this point because I realize I am straying ever so slightly from the bill itself, but I am saying this because I think that if we were ever to get the impression that by doing this we have done anything meaningful, then we would be fooling ourselves. If we were to get the impression that we can now sit back because we have made some reforms to the
April 30, 1982

Canada Elections Act, then we would be deluding ourselves. If we were ever to think that by virtue of having done this we might encourage a great deal more participation by the average citizen, who today looks with a jaundiced eye at the goings on in Parliament, then we are living in a fool's paradise. We have so much more to do, and the direction in which we are heading is not encouraging.
We are great technicians and can make things more technical or less technical, but we do not seem to be making them more relevant. I think relevance is a lot more important in the parliamentary process than whether it is set out in a way which will allow it to operate effectively. I think Parliament is irrelevant, not because I wish it to be that way-therefore I do not sound like the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in that regard. I want it to be more relevant. In all fairness, it is irrelevant for most Canadians; Parliament never deals with the things they believe to be important. I do not think they doubt our willingness, but I think they doubt our capacity and opportunity to deal with the important social and economic problems which confront them. With that in mind, I would urge the House that we not stop there, but that we also get on with the job of making this place function properly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for once I am completely in agreement with the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). I think his comments are important, and I am delighted he made them.
This bill, the purpose of which is simply to shorten the election period, does not even approach the election process in the manner it should. I also agree that there are larger reforms of this House to be made, but there are no signs that the government is going to convene the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization where we could address ourselves to the reforms needed to make this a more meaningful institution and restore the credibility it once had. This credibility is sadly lacking as a result of the inability of members to come to grips with the important issues of the day by virtue of the government's bringing forward what is sometimes rather negligible legislation.
I think in the eyes of many, this House is irrelevant because we have shown ourselves unable to deal with the major issues confronting the nation. I think this House could deal with the issues of inflation, unemployment and excessive interest rates, but it is not being given the opportunity because of the government's attitude towards these very problems.
To narrow the focus of my remarks, this bill does not attempt to deal in any broad way with the Canada Elections Act. To start with, Clause 5 of the bill amends Section 18(9) of the act whereby:
Each returning officer shall send a notice of enumeration in the prescribed form, not later than Wednesday, the twenty-sixth day before polling day, to each elector residing in a polling division in his electoral district whose name appeared on the preliminary list of electors for that polling division.
I am sure that was written before the 30-cent stamp came out. I would suggest that instead of calling this "an act to amend the Canada Elections Act", we might call it the "Canada Post relief act" because with some 12 million to 15 million voters this will mean a subsidy to the post office of around $4 million for the privilege of carrying these individual notices to
Canada Elections Act
the voters. I am sure there is no provision that where the names appear under the same address, they be mailed together.
I say that somewhat facetiously, but it is necessary to draw attention to that very important aspect of this bill. In addition to the expense of enumeration, printing the roll and so on, we are going to incur this extra cost.
That brings me to the matter of the enumerated roll. Although I attend a fair number of House committees, obviously I cannot get to them all, and I was unable to attend the Committee on Privileges and Elections which considered this bill. I have not followed the proceedings so I do not know whether an attempt was made to consider the possibility of a permanent voters' roll, which is maintained in many provinces including my own. The argument that we always get is that a permanent roll costs too much. However, Mr. Speaker, I suspect that if we could persuade the bureaucracy and one another that a permanent roll was a feasible proposition, we would save at least this $4-million subsidy to Canada Post because it would be the voters' obligation to check. Let us say that on the second day of January and the second day of July of each year voters should go to the municipal office nearest to them, for example, to make sure their names are on the list. If they do not, and an election is called, I say it is just tough. The first duty of an elector is to make sure that he or she is in a position to cast a ballot. The second duty, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, is that he cast it in accordance with the law. I see no problem at all with a permanent voters' list. I regret that there is no consideration of that subject in the bill before us.
There are a number of other matters that a bill amending the Canada Elections Act ought to have considered, matters which have been brought to the attention of the committee, to members, to the federal government and to other governments.
A number of other matters become clearly outlined to us in the course of an election but as the election recedes in our memories, some of them disappear. I do not want them to disappear. I want them to be remembered and incorporated in a bill. One of the most important ones for my money is that of mobile polls. They have mobile polls provincially. They have vans manned with polling officers, scrutineers and ballot boxes. These vans go from hospital to hospital, to homes for the elderly or to those at home in bed who cannot get out to vote. What about those people who did not think it necessary to go to the advance poll but were stricken by an illness or some other misfortune between the end of the advance poll and voting day? They are entitled to vote just the same. The polling officer should have a means to get the ballot box to them.
