speechtext: Is that an innovation?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
It is not an innovation, Mr. Speaker. I have brought that suggestion forward and I am

April 30, 1982
Canada Elections Act
sure others have done so too. The principle was taken to the committee, but it was ruled out as being impractical. It is not impractical. The bureaucracy would find it cumbersome perhaps. But there is a difference between its being cumbersome for the bureaucracy and its practicality. Not only is it practical, but I think it is essential in a democratic community. There must be some provision to enable those who are prevented because of illness, age, frailty or whatever to cast their vote. I regret that this bill, which claims to be dealing with amendments to the Canada Elections Act, has failed to take that into account.
Another matter I remember distinctly, which I have mentioned before and will go on mentioning, is the ability to vote at polling stations from the very earliest moment. This would be facilitated if we had a permanent voters' list. The voters' list would be in the hands of the returning officer in the polling station on the first day after the writ was issued. These days people have to make long-range plans for holidays so as to take advantage of air fares. They may have booked three or four months ahead. They may have had to leave the day before an election is held or the day before the advance poll opens or even the day before they can go to the returning office to cast their ballots. Therefore, there ought to be full provision for electors to go to the returning office to cast their ballots from the earliest possible moment. The returning officer, of course, must be given a day or two to get organized. But from then on until the advance poll, properly speaking, is organized, electors should be able to go to the returning office and vote and have their names removed from the roll. When the polls are eventually opened on election day those who have voted will be taken off the electoral rolls.
The matter of proxy vote is another matter. My recollection about that, and it is getting a little dim after the number of months which have now elapsed since the last election, is that there is provision in the law for only one person to become a proxy for an elector who may be disabled or otherwise unable to get out to vote. But in a very cumbersome manner a proxy can vote on behalf of only one other person. But the situation may very well be that of an elderly couple both of whom are on the electoral roll. Why should the proxy not be able to vote for both of them instead of having two proxies? I see the unreasonableness of having the single proxy, but 1 do not see why it should be beyond the scope of human intelligence or trust-it may be a matter of trust in an electoral situation for one person to become the proxy for two, three or four people-but what about a home for the elderly? There may be four people who cannot get out to vote. One individual should be able to become a proxy for all of them.
There is another extraordinary situation. I cannot understand the rationale behind it nor have I been able to get the situation changed. If you live in the rural part of a constituency and your name is on a rural poll, you can have a neighbour go with you to the polling office and that neighbour can swear you are who you are if your name is not on the roll. When that is done, your name is included on the roll. But in an urban situation, that cannot be done. That is nonsense. It is sheer nonsense. Why should there not be someone able to swear who you are? If you do not want a neighbour to do it, perhaps
someone with notary power or a justice of the peace can do it. Maybe for the purposes of the act, we could make the polling officer a justice of the peace for the day. Then a person could swear he is who he says he is. He would, of course, have to produce identification. The situation I am talking about is that of the enumerator's roll. I would much prefer to see a permanent roll. Nevertheless, in the case of an enumerator's roll, the person could swear that he is who he says he is and that he has lived for the prescribed time in the riding, is therefore entitled to vote and can vote. People can do this if they live in the rural part of the constituency but not if they live in the urban part of the constituency. In my opinion, that is sheer nonsence. Why does this bill not deal with that problem? This bill deals simply with reducing the number of days in an election campaign.
There is another circumstance that comes to mind, which I have seen take place many times. I am sure every member in this House who does his constituency duty on election day by visiting the polls to see if there is anything that can be done finds many people showing up at the wrong poll. The polling officer is not always sure where these people ought to be. People ask where they can go to cast their ballots if they are at the wrong place. First, I would suggest there ought to be a full voters' list, either enumerated or a permanent one in each polling station in the hands of the polling clerk. In addition, there should be a map of the entire riding, properly marked off so that a person having found his name can look at the map and say "I thought I voted here because I live on the boundary, but I see that I should be voting over there." For instance, let us say a person lives in Sidney, but should be in the North Saanich area and finds that he should be voting in McTavish. It is then a very simple matter. But sometimes people come from work to vote. It may be 6.30 p.m. or 7 p.m. before they arrive to vote. When they find they are in the wrong place, they realize they may miss the vote because they will never make it to the other polling station which might be some distance away. It may happen that it takes too long to find out where they should be voting. I suggest, therefore, that a full map of the riding be put in every polling station along with a complete roll of the voters in a constituency. Either the polling officer or someone else at the polling station can then help them.
Although I do not want to hold this bill up, I am quite upset that it does so little. I suppose what limited provisions there are in it should be passed on to the Senate for consideration.
However, I do not believe that we should be required to debate a bill which has such a narrow purpose, which is to simply shorten the length of an election period, when there are so many other equally important matters in the Canada Elections Act which require reform.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in my remarks and will indicate that I would like to register my support for this bill.
April 30, 1982

I recall, during second reading of this bill, that I went into some detail on matters pertaining to electoral reform and pointed out some provisions which should have been included. I will not repeat those today. One of the arguments made by some members of the opposition in favour of longer election periods was that a shorter period would tend to favour the incumbents. Since the government of the day would have more incumbents than the opposition, they would get the vote.
The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) has demonstrated this afternoon that this was not the case in Saskatchewan or Manitoba. I believe that as long as the campaign lasts for a least 25 days, a shorter period will have no bearing on an election outcome. Although we saw the government of two provinces change, it was not typical of a shorter election campaign. This can be evidenced by the Newfoundland experience.
Longer election periods in excess of two months were necessary in the early days of confederation when politicians were required to travel across the country by train and to the outlying areas by horsedrawn vehicles. However, with today's instant electronic communication via television and radio, it is not necessary. Even the printed word can be produced very quickly. For example, I recently visited a printing plant in my constiuency and was shown a machine which could print 2,000 copies of anything a customer wanted in ten minutes. Therefore, it does not require long periods of time in order to produce hand bills and other election material.
The primary reason why I suport a reduction in the election period is that it appears to be the wish of the voters and those who have to suffer us politicians through long election campaigns.
During elections in which I was a candidate, people would tell me two weeks before voting day that they were sick and tired of listening to politicians repeating their arguments and hearing them once again every time they would turn on their televisions. They had either made up their mind several days before or they had no intention of making up their mind until they walked into the polling booth. We should show some mercy to the voting public of Canada by not bombarding them with these electoral messages day in and day out, ad nauseam. We should give them a rest and reduce the period of the election campaign to at least the 50 days suggested in this bill.
Another problem concerns enumeration, one which has been pointed out by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) and other members who have spoken to this bill this afternoon. There are probably more complaints with regard to enumeration than any other electoral process. People complain because they are either not on the voting list or are on the wrong one and end up in the wrong polling station. Since people are frequently not at home when the enumerator calls, they fail to be properly enumerated. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain pointed out that this is particularly true because both parents are working and the children are at school.
There could be two approaches taken to the problem of enumeration. One solution was suggested by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) which was to establish a permanent voters' list. This system has worked successfully in
Canada Elections Act
some jurisdictions and it may be appropriate to adopt that procedure in Canada. At least it warrants more careful study.
Another system would involve eliminating a voters' list entirely. In a number of countries, as is the case in some rural areas of Canada, voters just attend the polling station, identify themselves and are then allowed to vote. In some countries after being sworn in, are stamped with indelible ink so that they cannot vote again. Perhaps we could use a system similar to that. It is similar to having your hand stamped when you go to a social function, thus allowing you to leave the room and then return to it. The election system would perhaps be more sophisticated but the notion of enabling everyone to vote only once is workable.
My last point concerns the appointment of election officials. I am not in favour of the existing system whereby the government in power may appoint the returning officers and deputy returning officers. Its smacks too much of patronage.
As an illustration, just this morning I read a volume of correspondence written by Sir John A. Macdonald. One of the letters in that file was to one of his supporters who was running for office. The gist of the letter indicated that Sir John A. Macdonald had been fortunate enough, in his opinion, to secure the services of a certain returning officer who, he thought, would be favourable towards this particular candidate. This happened approximately 100 years ago. I do not know whether it happens as blatantly today, but I would not put it past some of our friends on the other side of the House.
I have another story about Sir John A. Macdonald and elections. In the old Northwest Territories, before the government stole Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba from us, the lieutenant governor of the day sent a wire to Sir John A. Macdonald concerning the fact that one of the requirements for a voter was that he should be a householder. This was before universal enfranchisement when women were given the right to vote. The question asked by the lieutenant governor was whether people living in teepees should be considered as householders for voting purposes. Of course, the reply was; yes, if they were Conservatives.
In any event, it is my contention that the appointment of electoral officials, returning officers, deputy returning officers and all those officials required to conduct an election should be appointed by and be under the direct control of the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada. I believe that he has made that recommendation himself on several occasions, and he has my support for it and, I would think, the support of many other members as well.
Let me say in conclusion that I will be pleased to support this proposed legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to say that I listened to the last speech, which was given by my colleague, the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) and I enjoyed it very much. The people in the north have a peculiar problem which you and I do not face, as

Canada Elections Act
Your Honour, lives in an urban area and I live in a suburban area of the national capital. This problem is not present in Toronto, but 1 suppose something akin to it can be found in some western ridings, and especially the northern parts of Saskatchean, Alberta and British Columbia. If one were to review the minutes of the committees, one would find that those questions and differences have all been addressed. We all hope that the short period set forth in this bill is a reasonable compromise. Therefore, I join with my friends from all over the country to say that I hope this new compromise works.
Speaking personally for a moment as a candidate in four elections, I want to say that the previous election period seemed to be very long indeed. It must be murder for party leaders who travel the country by airplane, going through time changes, time zones, hours of darkness and hours of light, adjusting eating schedules and doing all of the things they must do in order to maintain some semblance of strength and mental order so that they can carry on from place to place. The problems are tremendous. In a period of time when we seem to have the advantages, if they can be called that, of almost instantaneous communication, it is well that we consider this bill and the propositions it sets forth.
As I say, I believe the bill is a reasonable compromise. I do not think we should end our consideration of elections and representation in the House of Commons by saying that we can deal only with time, that we can merely deal with the posting of notices and the shortening of election periods. There are some other matters which are crucial to all of us who are interested in the House of Commons. I regret that some of the problems which have occurred and are likely to occur are problems which have come about by neglect, or perhaps by allowing this House to grow like Topsy. Perhaps this has created problems for members of Parliament in many ways. However, I want to deal with some of the relevant problems when we consider any change in the electoral process. The result of the present electoral process means that at least 282 men and women are sent here to represent Canadians from various parts of the country. This Parliament is a very complex institution. Its wellbeing is affected by many factors beyond the internal rules it sets for itself or the different personalities of which it is composed.
During my period of office as president of the Privy Council, I proposed many changes to the rules of the House of Commons. In the present session of Parliament, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) has promised rules reforms, but none have yet seemed to materialize. I say that regretfully. Strangely enough, an important change is about to be made in the House. It has really been unannounced and it is unwanted by many hon. members in the House. By the next election, there will be an additional 28 members of Parliament to be elected to the House, bringing it to a total of 310 seats. By the year 2001, which is only 20 years ahead, no matter how exotic it may sound, the membership of this House could leap up to the ludicrous total of 374 or 375.
These changes may very well be made without any discussion in the House because a loophole in the legislation required a committee to look into it. This situation had its origins in the
review of representation following the census in 1981. Keep it in mind that the British North America Act requires a new apportionment of seats after each decennial census. Under the law enforced to govern representation under which the size of the House of Commons was basically kept stable, Nova Scotia, Quebec, Manitoba and Newfoundland were to lose seats. This was considered to be unacceptable by members of Parliament from those provinces. Furthermore, it was unacceptable to certain MPs who were to lose their own seats under the terms of the new redistribution. One of those unahppy individuals was the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), then the president of the Privy Council and the minister responsible for electoral reform.
So what happened? The boundary readjustment was suspended and the whole issue was referred to a committee. Eventually, a new representation act was passed, embodying what came to be called the amalgam method. It was called that because it combined three different formulae for apportioning seats to small, medium and large provinces. More important, in connection with our present problem, it legislated that in the decennial readjustment of representation, no province was to lose seats. The province of Quebec was to become the basis of calculations for all the provinces. Quebec would have 75 seats, and four more seats would be added after every decennial census. The House would therefore grow very substantially every ten years.
In the federal election of 1979, the first under the new system, 18 new seats were added. The big winners were Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. Despite growth in Canada's population, the population of individual ridings had been held relatively constant as a result. The members of Parliament and the minority parliament of 19721974 knew very well that what they were doing was temporary and that they were dealing only with their own situations and were passing the general question as to whether provinces should see their representation eroded on to a new parliament. This is a new Parliament. In fact, this specific provision was included in the new Representation Act, 1974, requiring the House of Commons of 1979 to review the whole formula for setting the number of seats and distributing them among the provinces. I would like to quote the section of the act which calls for that review. Section 7 of the said act states:
The President of the Privy Council shall,
(a)	on a day not later than the twentieth sitting day of the House of Commons
after the 30th day of June, 1979, if there is then an existing Parliament, or
(b)	if there is not then an existing Parliament, on a day not later than the
twenty-fifth sitting day of the House of Commons after Parliament has been
summoned,
propose to the House of Commons that an order be made and referred to the appropriate committee of the House of Commons for the review by that committee of the Rules provided by subsection 51(1) of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1974, as amended by the British North America Act (No. 2), 1974, and for the recommendations of such committee with respect to any amendments, alterations or modifications thereto that appear to the committee then to be necessary or desirable, and upon such order being referred to it the committee shall consider the matter of the order and report to the House its recommendations with respect thereto.
April 30, 1982

That is delightful draftsman's language. If Your Honour could decipher it, you would realize that the review was to be commenced in the early fall of 1979, even if an election came before the reference could be proposed to the House. I emphasize the word "proposed". A committee was then to hold a thorough review and report to the House. In other words, Parliament in 1974 wanted the House in 1979 to catch the hot potato it was passing on and figure out whether or not it was wise to let the House go on growing.
Unfortunately, the draftsman provided for every contingency but the one which occurred. In the fall of 1979 I, as president of the Privy Council, did propose such a motion to the House. Debate on this committee reference was indeed begun before the twenty-fifth sitting day had elapsed, on November 12, 1979. A detailed discussion paper was being prepared by my officials to assist at committee. That paper set out a number of alternatives to the unrestrained growth of the House of Commons.
Before the reference could be debated further, the House fell and the government changed. No more has been heard of a review of the 1974 Representation Act. The 1981 census has now come and gone. The redistribution that I have spoken about and the number of seats that the process commenced is pretty well fixed in stone, unless there is some other sculptor to change the etching on that stone.
In the most technical sense the requirements of the act have been met. A reference was proposed and called for debate. If the reference lapses, so do all the provisions for the committee review based on that reference. The nullification of the review provisions by a new election was not foreseen by the original draftsman of the Representation Act. Nor did they foresee that a government would happily let this House become a bloated monstrosity without any comment from its members. Rather than address the difficult questions faced and then avoided in 1974 for the reasons 1 have given, the government has decided to avoid them again. I hear nothing about this question now. Worse still, there is no further review of this reckless growth scheduled under the act. All the brakes now seem to be off.
The potential exists, not only for the House to grow after a few decades to the size of the British House of Commons at 635 members but to ultimately surpass it, because there is no end in sight to this growth under the formula at the moment.
What will happen to the Canadian House of Commons if every ten years it grows by about 30 members of Parliament? We are already at our physical limit. To accommodate the new 18 members in 1979, the Speaker's chair was moved right back to the press gallery wall and all the aisles between the seats were made narrower. If we have 30 more members in this House, we will have to replace the desks with benches, knock out the walls or eliminate the aisles altogether and use cranes to lower members of Parliament into their benches.
The cost would be incredible. In 1979 my officials estimated that each additional MP resulted directly in an expenditure of
Canada Elections Act
$140,000 in personal and staff salaries. That would be between $170,000 and $190,000 today. The indirect costs are probably more frightening. In the last 20 years the House has taken over the West Block, the Confederation Building, the Metropolitan Life Building, the East Block, and has rented floor space in a few other buildings. By the time the new Royal Bank building on Sparks Street is ready, we will have to take it as well if there are more members added to the House.
I believe the impact on the operation of the House will be devastating. It is already difficult for many backbenchers to be recognized during question period or during a major debate. More and more members of considerable talent feel that the line-up for a cabinet position or some other key role is already too long. It is too easy to waste years as an MP in waiting. It is incredible to think that a major expansion of the House with all its physical, economic and even its psychological implications will be allowed to take place without a word from those most affected.
There are very serious questions to be addressed by the House of Commons and by the government. Do we want to let the House continue to grow and, if so, by how much? Is it reasonable to try to keep constituencies at the same population level or should we expand staff and technical resources instead of the House itself? Can we allow provinces to lose seats if they lag behind in population growth?
Is Quebec, as the home of most of Canada's French-speaking population a special case? Should there be a floor below which no province can fall, and how should that floor be set? Do provinces gain much if instead of actually losing seats they merely retain a fixed representation while other provinces gain more and more seats?
The answer so far has been to solve this problem by negligence. The House will grow and the people will pay more politicians and the frustrations of parliamentary life will grow as well. I believe the government must honour the spirit of the law and refer this matter to a committee. It should stay referred there so that we can hear from the members of the House of Commons who are interested in the operation of this place. Those cabinet papers that I had should be put there so this whole matter can be considered. It has already wasted time. The census has passed. Unless this Parliament acts, we are going to start this mathematical progression to monstrous proportions in terms of the House.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your indulgence in allowing me to speak to this matter. I feel it is important. It is just as important for the operation of this House of Commons that we consider how we are, how many there should be, what resources we should have, what service should be available to us in our representational capacity and how we can function, as it is to consider how many days we should take to get here. That is the contribution I want to make to this debate. I thank hon. members. I hope they will consider what I have said because it is very important to our wellbeing in the House.
May I call it four o'clock Mr. Speaker?

April 30, 1982
Public Service

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext:
that Bill C-297, to amend the Public Service Employment Act and the Public Service Staff Relations Act (political rights), be read the
second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: I thank the House for the opportunity to present this bill. I have had it on the order paper for a number of years and I have been lucky in the draw, or the session of Parliament has lasted long enough, that we have reached Bill C-297. It is always appropriate to debate this kind of subject, but it is more appropriate now, since tomorrow is May Day. Around the world, workers celebrate May Day.
All of us have good intentions about the rights of people generally but these good intentions do not go for much if they are not backed up by actions. The best current example we have at the moment is the situation in Poland where people are denied the fundamental freedom of expression. Members of all parties in the House have spoken passionately and sincerely in support of those kinds of rights-for El Salvador, for Argentina-wherever human rights are denied. The Canadian situation is not as extreme but I hope members will recognize the need for political rights for federal public servants of the same kind that all other citizens of Canada have.
The Civil Service Act of 1913 contained a provision, virtually unchanged to this day, severely limiting the civil rights of federal employees. Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act is headed "Political Partisanship". My bill changes this offensive heading to read "Political Rights".
Clause 1 of the bill would prevent discrimination in employment for political allegiance or activity.
Clause 2 of the bill sets out the political rights of employees who, under existing legislation, can be fired for political activities for or against candidates or parties seeking office. This bill would allow employees to engage in political activity on their own time, when they are off duty, or if they take holidays with pay or get leave of absence without pay. It would allow an employee to take leave of absence to be a candidate in an election-federal, provincial or municipal. An employee elected in such an election would automatically be on leave of absence for up to five years. I am talking about those who come under the Public Service Commission.
I agree that employees who are employed under orders in council or on contract are in an entirely different category. I do not expect a Liberal government to hire a Conservative or a member of the New Democratic Party to be a deputy minister or a branch head or the head of a Crown corporation. I do not expect the government in power to hire somebody to be in a position either to draft or be responsible for implementing a policy with which he does not agree. It is perfectly legitimate,
April 30, 1982

in my opinion, when governments change, for the new administration to bring in people it wants to hold the highest office in the Public Service to draft and to implement the policies of the government of that day. So I am not talking about those who are order in council employees or who work for the government under contract.
Under the existing Public Service Staff Relations Act, public service unions-even the unions-are not allowed to use membership money for political purposes, even if the membership votes overwhelmingly or unanimously to spend some of their money for political purposes. The union itself is barred from doing that. Yet all other unions can do it at any time they want, for any political party. Any organization or association can do it at any time they wish. There is a legislative prohibition against the Public Service unions. Even if they unanimously vote to spend some of their money for political purposes of whatever nature, they can be decertified. Surely that is not fair.
My bill would give Public Service unions the same rights and privileges as have all other unions in Canada-or for that matter all other organizations and associations who choose to spend money for political purposes.
Civil servants, those who are appointed by orders in council or are under contract, can still exercise their political rights; but they will have to take their chances. There will always be people in positions of high responsibility, and the secrecy of government discussions and so forth must be maintained. All the others should have the same rights as other Canadians, the same political freedom to decide whether or not they want to donate money individually or through their unions to a political party or to a candidate.
I would like to remind the House, Mr. Speaker, that when a person takes employment in the Public Service each employee takes an oath of office and secrecy which says:
I will faithfully and honestly fulfil the duties that devolve upon me by reason of my employment in the Public Service and that I will not, without due authority in that behalf, disclose or make known any matter that comes to my knowledge by reason of such employment.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is a sufficient safeguard for any legislative body or government. Why, then, with the requirement that that kind of an oath be taken, would any government want to restrict the political rights of its own employees? Surely that safeguard is in place and it is sufficient?
Political rights for civil service employees have worked in practice, although five provinces in this country still deny political rights, they being Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec. The other five allow various larger degrees of freedom than we presently have in the federal statutes. The experiences have been good. In Saskatchewan an employee cannot be forced to engage in political work nor can he be discriminated against for taking part in political activity. British Columbia probably has the best legislation. Employees can be granted leave without pay to serve in an elective position for up to five years and can be granted leave without pay to be a candidate. There are no restrictions, other than the oath of office, for employees of the B.C. government who engage in political activities in their own time. I say that the experience has been good, Mr. Speaker.
Public Service
1 have worked in, or run in, about 25 elections, federal and provincial, since 1952. I have seen public servants be candidates or campaign managers or organizers or canvassers. They could just put up a sign on the lawn. They were from all political parties, no matter what government was in power in my province.
I would like to illustrate that. When Mr. Douglas brought in legislation in 1945 guaranteeing political rights for public servants, there was a great deal of worry. But the experience was good. There were civil servants who wanted leave to work on behalf of the Liberals, the Tories, the NDP, the CCF or Social Credit. They returned to their jobs and they carried out their duties conscientiously.
I do not know of a single instance where a public servant who took part in political party activity in his own time, who was not of the persuasion of the party in power in Saskatchewan, who would ever in any way either betray or work against the duties that he was required to do in his employment.
After we were defeated in 1964 and there were five former CCF MLAs working for Crown corporations or government departments, the new premier, Mr. Thatcher, did not fire them. He kept them working. He told them quite frankly that as long as they did their jobs conscientiously and did not do any CCFing while they were on duty, there would be no problem. Similarly, when Mr. Blakeney took power in 1971, two former Liberal candidates in the employ of the provincial government were not fired. Both of them kept working for a number of years. In fact, I think one of them is still working in a government department. They did their jobs conscientiously and properly and retained their political rights. For all I know, one or both of them might end up being candidates for the Liberal party again, although that would not be a good idea in Saskatchewan at the moment. At any event, the experience has been good.
Bill C-297 might not be the perfect solution. Even if hon. members on all sides do not agree entirely with the details of my bill, I ask the House to pass it-preferably-let it go at second reading and let it go to the appropriate committee of Parliament so that a committee of the House can examine it and come back with a recommendation. If the bill does not pass now at second reading I hope hon. members will at least let the subject matter of the bill be referred to the appropriate standing committee of Parliament because this is putting action where our words are. This is following up on what is being done in other places and what is in our Constitution. In fact, it is very possible that a federal government or a provincial government could find itself in court because of a denial of the rights and freedoms contained in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in our new Constitution, and I do not think even this government wants to work that hard at causing trouble for itself.
Surely, what I ask for is nothing more than simple justice and propriety on the part of this Parliament and the government to ensure that the political rights within the framework

April 30, 1982
Public Service
defined in my bill are enshrined in the law of this land for our public servants. I am confident that no matter what party is in power the experience will be like that which we have had in Saskatchewan and British Columbia. The experience will be good. In fact, I suspect we will get even better work and performance out of our public servants.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak about this matter for just a few moments because it is something which has troubled me a great deal and occupied some time in the House of Commons.
I will not suggest-the hon. member who has just spoken also noted this-that we might agree with every clause, every comma and every jot in his bill, but I think the bill raises some very important questions which are quite pertinent at the moment and which, I believe, should be addressed by the House of Commons. We are talking about something which is quite fundamental. As my friend, the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), has just mentioned, we dealt with the Constitution a few days ago. It was proclaimed by Her Majesty the Queen on April 17 when she was here in Ottawa, and the question of the rights of public servants has engaged the House, but it is likely to engage us in a new sense, a constitutional sense, as we go on to consider political rights, democratic rights, equality rights and the application of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We will have to find out what the Charter means, and I do not think it would hurt to begin that examination in a parliamentary committee. If the House saw fit today to refer this bill to a House committee to deal with it, I would cheer. I would cheer even if my friend were to propose-as he did-that the subject matter of the bill go to a committee. I would be quite prepared to move that kind of motion if that were acceptable to him-

speechtext:
I do not propose to speak at length about the bill, and I do not propose to refer to it in relation to a case which has just now been heard under the law with respect to one particular public servant. However, that case has disturbed me because it has raised some real questions in my mind about the state of the law at the moment.
Political rights of public servants are governed by Section 32 of their statute, and that section has caused me to write to the chairman of the Public Service Commission on one occasion. I wrote to him and asked him about how that section might apply. Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act deals with the political rights of people and says that a person does not contravene the limitations by reason only of his attending a political meeting or contributing money for the funds of a candidate for election as a member or money for the funds of a political party. Then it goes on to talk about the rights of
public servants to make applications. What it says, interestingly enough, is that a person can belong to a political party, he can go to a meeting, he can give money and he can do everything else everyone else in the country can do, but he does not have the right to speak. According to the chairman of the Public Service Commission, he does not have the right to speak by putting a sign on his lawn or to speak in the course of a political discussion.
Neil Fraser and another public servant in eastern Canada who headed a committee dealing with the compensation to be paid UFFI victims were told they could not speak even about matters which did not deal directly with their departments but which were political to the extent that they were programs of the government. I think we have a real problem on our hands, and I do not think the second reading stage of debate in the House of Commons is the time to consider that problem. However, I do believe it is time we faced up to things and had this subject matter before a committee of the House of Commons.
With respect to political rights, I am a member of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, and that committee had before it one night Mr. Edgar Gallant, the chairman of the Public Service Commission, and the next day the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) appeared to discuss this matter. We were discussing it in terms of the fact that in Canada there is no comprehensive codified system yet developed which would apply to all situations for all public servants and employees of Crown corporations, ministers, members of Parliament and so forth. There is nothing. There is no code of ethics. There is no code of conduct. There are some old oaths around relating to one's duties to the programs in one's department, but there is nothing general.
I put a question to the chairman of the Public Service Commission when he was there. Knowing his view that codification may not be the best way, I asked him whether he thought the time had now come when we should review this matter. I asked him if he thought it is an appropriate time for this whole question to go to a parliamentary committee. The chairman, quite honestly and forthrightly, as is usual for him when he is asked questions by members in committee, said, "Yes, I do think it is time this matter was discussed". It was raised in the context of the Neil Fraser case because that was on everyone's mind. It was not pursued in that context because it goes far beyond the elements of that case.
Next day the President of the Treasury Board appeared before the committee and I put the same general question to him and asked how he felt about it. He said he had no objection to the parliamentary committee dealing with the question and that he would consult his colleagues. I gave him a reasonable amount of time to do that. I gather from his answer in the House a few days ago that he is still consulting them or, if he has consulted them, they have not responded yet. I think the government should respond. It could do so today if it wished.

April 30, 1982

The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that with respect to matters political, civil servants can only talk philosophy. You know, Mr. Speaker, how profitable a discussion on matters of philosophy can be. Sometimes we think the problem with the government is that it discusses philosophy rather than practical matters.
There is no statute law that prohibits the conduct that has given rise to the debate before the committee. I wonder if in the Fraser case or perhaps the case of the employees of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), the government would have moved so swiftly if the issue being criticized on those occasions was not metric, bilingualism, the Constitution and a few other things but had been criticism of the slowness of the government to act on the freedom of information policy. If Neil Fraser had been criticizing the government on that, I wonder if they would have thought him an ally and done nothing about what he said.
After I put a question to the President of the Treasury Board on February 24 in the House, he admitted to reporters outside the House that the situation of public servants might not be so clear. In fact, he called it a "grey area". Yet he refused to intervene against the dismissal of one public servant who had to be left to his own devices.
The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) has said that it is quite permissible for a public servant to speak out and advocate and market programs, even though such programs may be the subject of partisan political debate in the country. That is permissible. A public servant can speak in favour of partisan issues that the government likes but cannot speak against partisan issues that the government does not like. There is a double standard there that should be examined.
The public service of 1982 is not the public service of 1918. It may have escaped the notice of the government, but in the intervening years unions have been allowed in the public service sector, public servants can belong to political parties, and they can stand as candidates in an election. So the evolution in Canada, as in the rest of the world until this case came up, has been in favour of freedom and openness rather than restriction.
Of course a public servant cannot openly criticize the policy of his department, but is he prohibited from expressing himself in other areas of public policy which affect him personally? For instance, if his house is insulated with urea formaldehyde, can he join a group that is intent on attacking the policy of compensation of the government, with impunity? If he feels abused by the government's high interest rate policy, can he march on Parliament Hill with other Canadians, when his unions and affiliates have arranged such a march, as they did?
The example of the senior officer in a firm in the private sector that was used by the President of the Treasury Board when he answered my question on February 24 in the House, was not very helpful. Of course, if that senior person was publicly critical of his firm's policy, then I think this dismissal might be justified. But is there a reasonable case for dismissal if such a man or woman said nothing about the policy of his firm-let us assume it was a law firm-but was critical of the Law Society of Upper Canada? Or if an employee of Mitel
Public Service
was not critical of Mitel but had something to say about the Canadian Association of Advanced Technology?
The practice of government has changed as well. The Liberal government spends millions of dollars advertising programs and policies even before they are passed by Parliament. In 1982, then, are public servants risking dismissal if they write to their MP and urge him not to support, say, a proposal in the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) which deals with pensions? I do not think so.
Clearly, then, the case that is engaging the attention of the public, the Fraser case and the other cases that have been referred to, illustrate just how dangerous it is to accept without question the views of the government on the matter. They also illustrate just how important it is that there be some way that this issue can be examined by a parliamentary committee and how important it is that this bill receive the appropriate approval of the House and that the subject matter go to committee.
As the rules stand now, they are unclear and their enforcement is uneven. I believe it is within the capability of Parliament to at least attempt to clear up some of the confusion.
If this bill is helpful, and I believe it can be, to clear up matters that deal with the rights of unions, which are of concern to the hon. member and myself, because that atmosphere is changing as well, then it is equally important that it be used as a vehicle to deal with questions regarding employees of the government and their rights.
In today's mail I received a copy of a letter from a Mr. John L. Fryer, President of the National Union of Provincial Government Employees, which was directed to the President of the Treasury Board. It reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Johnston:
A month has passed since it was reported in the Ottawa Citizen that you had endorsed the proposal to give a Parliamentary Committee the job of trying to clarify the political rights of public servants.
I wrote to you on March 30th commending you on this decision and on April 7th I received acknowledgement of my letter from your Correspondence Coordinator.
Upon enquiring of your office and others it would appear that there is still no Committee and still no terms of reference respecting this very important issue.
Again I wish to advise you that this matter is of major importance to public service employees both in the Federal and Provincial jurisdictions. We deem it a most worth-while exercise to have these political rights clarified for the benefit of the employees themselves as well as the politicians and the public generally.
I urge you to press forward with the formation of this Parliamentary Committee so that it can get on with this most important task.
Today is the day, Mr. Speaker. If the President of the Treasury Board meant what he said, if the words and views of the Chairman of the Public Service Commission are to have life breathed into them, then the time has come for study. Today is the day. Today is the day when a former minister of this government, the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), or the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Cousineau), can get on their feet on behalf of this government and say: "ready, aye ready; let us examine the program and use the bill of the hon. member for Regina as a vehicle to do it."

speechtext: Don't talk this bill out.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext:
I promise 1 will not talk the bill out, Mr. Speaker. I hope the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) or the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Cousineau) will not either. They would certainly be doing their constituents a disfavour were they to attempt to do so.
I am pleased that the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) has brought this matter to our attention. I will not speak very long on this bill, but I would like to say that in principle I support the idea of having this subject referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates so that it can be looked at in detail. I find a little difficulty with some of the wording, but the thought and the principle behind this bill are good. It is a matter worthy of detailed consideration and serious study in committee.
Like the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), I represent an area where there are many public servants, both at the federal and at the more junior levels. You run up against some very funny things in areas like this. In some areas where almost all the population works directly for the public service, or they have family members who do, it is very hard to get any kind of a political discussion going. It is pretty hard to get assistance for any political party in an election because people are afraid of losing their jobs. They themselves do not know what their rights are. I ran up against an example of that a couple of elections ago when we wished to hire a band to play at an election rally. I am sure the other political parties were trying to do precisely the same thing and probably would have been quite willing to hire the same band, but band members felt that, because their full-time job was in the public service, they could not even do that. They could not play music at a political meeting because in some way their supervisor might not like what happened and they feared for their jobs, An extreme example, I am sure, but a very common problem.
In every election campaign in the area which I represent, whether it be federal, territorial or even municipal, this question always comes up. At all political meetings people want to know what the candidates feel about the matter of political rights for public servants. It has been an issue for many years. I understand that at the territorial level in the Yukon they have come up with some pretty good legislation granting certain political rights to certain classes of public servants. If this matter gets to committee I would suggest the Yukon legislation dealing with this matter be looked at because it appears to have worked reasonably well in that jurisdiction.
I have been requested by many of my constituents to have this matter discussed openly in Parliament so that they will know where they stand. By and large the opinion of public servants is that they would like more political rights. Some people who are not public servants are worried about going too far in that direction. Although they support public servants having a certain amount of political rights, they see a line across which you should not go. One of the difficulties we face in this subject is defining where public servants may get really
involved in the political process and where they should not become at all involved. Obviously if you are a deputy minister you should stay away from partisan activities. In no way should he be seen as an outright supporter of one political party or another. On the other hand, take a person who happens to be a bricklayer or drives a grader for the highways department. Obviously, there is no reason why that person should not be the president of a local political organization. There is no harm done there. But where do you draw the line?
If someone is dealing continuously on important topics with members of the general public and is known to be a strong supporter of a particular party, someone of another political stripe is going to be leery of dealing with that person. People in that kind of position should control what they do. Very often it is a question of a public servant determining in his own mind how far he can or should go in his overt political activities.
The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton cited changes in the public service since confederation. At one time only a small percentage of the working population was employed in the public service. It was something of an elite group, and in those times it was understood that if you got into this type of work you were prepared to give up some of the political rights that other people enjoyed. People could understand and live with that. But now, if you take public servants at the federal, provincial and municipal levels, and include Crown corporations, you probably end up with 35 per cent or 40 per cent of the working population employed by the government in one way or another. The situation is now entirely different because government makes up so much of the modern economy and it is almost impossible not to have someone in a family working for government one way or another. Therefore, we have to change our ideas as to the propriety of people being involved in political activity when they or their relatives are employed by the government. I would not like to see some 35 per cent or 40 per cent of the population excluded from exercising political rights which other people accept as being common.
I enjoyed listening to the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton because he broadened the question somewhat. He cited some recent occurrences which make it very important that these questions be addressed and resolved in the near future. It is not something we should let slip by. We should pursue it with diligence. There is a wider case than just partisan activity that has to be examined. I hope it can be looked at simultaneously when we look at this aspect in committee.
I am now turning over the floor to the hon. member for Gatineau and the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton so they can have ample opportunity to make representations without having to resort to talking out this bill. If they do not talk it out, I am sure we will have some very interesting discussions in committee.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) obviously did not
April 30, 1982

know there were others in the Elouse as interested in this particular reference as he is himself and as is the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). But I can assure you that 1 am very interested in this subject. Perhaps surprisingly to some and perhaps surprisingly to the hon. member for Western Arctic, I have been the victim of such a policy at an earlier point. From 1975 to 1979 I was a member of the public service in a senior executive category. When I decided to seek political office I approached the Public Service Commission to see if I could obtain a leave of absence to undertake political activities involving nomination leading to elected office. I was told at that time that I could not have a leave of absence. Being at a senior level in the public service I interacted with the minister. My impartiality as a public servant would be seriously called into question. For example, had I lost in 1979-which I did not-and had I been on a leave of absence only to return to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, I would have been faced at that time with a Conservative minister. That Conservative minister was part of a cabinet that would have included the individual I had defeated in Ottawa Centre. What an extremely precarious position it would have been for me to be in as a senior public servant!

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext: He would have kept you working.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext: Mr. de Cotret, who was the hon. member for Ottawa Centre and whom I defeated in 1979 was made a Senator. He was named to the cabinet and became a minister. The hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) was the minister of consumer and corporate affairs. The situation could arise where Mr. de Cotret and the minister of consumer and corporate affairs would be in a cabinet committee, which I attended from time to time as a public servant. 1 would be sitting across the table from a man I had defeated in Ottawa Centre.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext: What is wrong with that?

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext: You can imagine how much credibility I, as a public servant, would have had in the eyes of the particular minister. I would not have had very much credibility. I would suggest to you that my career as a public servant would have either ended rather abruptly had I received a leave of absence only to return to the public service, or the department, out of kindness, generosity and basic good sense, would have buried me as far away from ministers as they possibly could.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext: This bill will protect you.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext:
Should I have been allowed a leave of absence? The hon. member for Western Arctic raised that very point. At the same time as I ran for office another individual in the public service ran on behalf of the New Democratic Party against me in Ottawa Centre, but he did receive leave of absence. He works in the Public Archives and he has run as my opponent in Ottawa Centre in the last two elections. He was granted a leave of absence because he was not in a sensitive position. His position in the public service has not been affected. But that is a perfect example of the spectrum, where
Public Service
one person is in a position where he or she interacts with ministers and makes policy recommendations to ministers.
A public servant has to be objective, fair and impartial. Only in this manner can a minister have confidence in that person being completely politically impartial. But what about the situation of a public servant who does not interact, does not directly make policy, and who is not visible to the minister? The relationship between the minister and his or her department is not affected. 1 can see the need for that difference. But that raises another fundamental issue. What the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Benjamin) is discussing is equal rights for Canadians. I suggest that my rights are as important as the rights of an individual who works in the Archives and who ran for the New Democratic Party. But under any kind of system that we can visualize where we are not going to politicize the public service, my rights would have to be different from the rights of an individual in a different category or in a different type of job in the public service. No matter what you do, you will have situations where some public servants have rights and other public servants do not.
This leads into the question of why am I entering the public service? Is it my role as a public servant to make policy and to enter into public debate on public policy, or is it my job as a public servant to implement policy which has been made by the elected representatives of the people? I suggest that the public service is a very unique type of occupation. It is different from all others. Those of us here in the House, the hon. member for Western Arctic, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Cousineau) and the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) were elected by the people to be their representatives in the House of Commons and to make public policy. To do that effectively we have to have a body of people to implement public policy. There is a dramatic difference in roles, and that distinction and difference has to be maintained. First, there has to be a body of people which the electorate puts in place in the House of Commons to make public policy and there has to be a body of people who have to be totally impartial, not only from the point of view of politicians perceiving those public servants as being impartial, but they have to be impartial from the public who call upon the public servant to provide those services which they have every right to expect from the public servant.
I should say at this point that I agree with the hon. member for Nepean-carleton that this subject should be debated and it should be examined carefully. I am in favour of that. The discussions that I and the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton have had with the minister indicate that the minister is interested. The chairman of the Public Service Commission has told both the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton and me that this matter should be looked at. I am confident it will be. The minister is consulting with his cabinet colleagues on the matter. I am confident he will bring forward a reference to have the matter looked at.

But I think we have to go deeper than that. Today is a good day to debate whether or not there are distinct differences between those who are elected to make policy for the people on behalf of the people, and those who are elected to deliver those policies to the people. As I mentioned, there is a confidence factor from the point of view of us, as politicians, being able to depend on that advice, or at least having the perception that we depend on that advice. We should not have a knowledge that the advice may be biased or less than objective because of political persuasion. We have to depend on the public servants and we should not ask questions about their loyalty for one political party or another. Their careers could be in jeopardy as well.
My own example is a case in point. My career as a public servant would have been seriously jeopardized had I remained there or returned to it. I think all members can ask the question: if we were defeated in the next election would we feel comfortable going to work for the public service? There is a curious anomaly concerning the Public Service Employment Act. This question was raised with Mr. Gallant when I was applying for my leave of absence. This anomaly is that when applying for a position in the public service, the Public Service Commission cannot look behind your current application for previous political activities or affiliations. Political affiliation cannot be taken into consideration when a public servant is hired. This means that I could have left my position at Consumer and Corporate Affairs, resigned-as I did-and if 1 had been defeated I could have gone back to the Public Service Commission to apply for my old job, and they could not consider the fact that I had run in an election.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext: That is the way it should be.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT-PUBLIC SERVICE STAFF RELATIONS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLITICAL RIGHTS OF PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member. However, that raises a similar problem. I would have been in exactly the same position, sitting beside the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) in a cabinet committee meeting. In that case, had the member I ran against been elected, he would be sitting across the table from me. Therefore, there are some great anomalies.
Another question, apart from our confidence in public servants who act as politicians, concerns the confidence which the public has when they talk to a public servant that they will be treated with total impartiality and will receive good service, irrespective of what political stripe they may be. There should be no question in the mind of some, when talking to a public servant that if he is recognized to be of a different political stripe he will not get good or fast service. Instances of someone who knows a public servant and has fought with him on different sides in an election campaign, and therefore does not expect to have his problem dealt with quickly is just an example of some of the problems encountered.
The hon. member for Regina West should take note because there are other dangers as well which could result from overt political activity in the public service.
One of those problems is and will be experienced in Saskatchewan. With Saskatchewan's wide open public service it has been known that many of the public servants who worked in the Blakeney government have had strong political affiliations. Now that there is a Conservative government there, how confident is that Conservative premier and his government, which was overwhelmingly elected by the people, going to be in the advice they get from the public servants?
I suggest that we should examine very carefully that very situation over the next several months because if, as I suspect may be the case, the premier of Saskatchewan says that he is not confident that he is receiving the best advice, he may simply fire a large number of public servants through some means. We will then have seen an example of a situation which is totally contrary to the parliamentary traditions of this country and of the mother Parliament where public servants are impartial and not replaced when governments change. We can see the beginning of the over-all change in the nature of the public service. When these hearings, which I believe should be called, are held I suggest that some public servants be summoned to talk about that situation. They should be asked how they percieve their political activities and whether those activities will be potentially difficult for them. They have a right to have an opinion on what the rules will be. As well, we have a right to look into that situation. Therefore, I suggest that this matter be examined before the appropriate committee because it is a matter of great concern to my constituents in Ottawa Centre.
I think that I have perhaps played the devil's advocate today in reviewing what is perhaps the downside of political activity. However, my constituents have indicated that they would like more political freedom to put signs on their lawns, for instance, something with which I do not see any great difficulty. People do that anyway. If a man who works in the public service displays a political sign he simply says that it belongs to his wife, or vice versa. If they both work in the public service they just say that the sign belongs to their son or daughter. This is an example of some of the archaic rules which exist in the Public Service Employment Act, which I do not believe have any major application.
However, there are some fundamental questions that politicians, and public servants who advise us, must deal with together in order to establish a fair set of rules which will allow the type of political activity that our constituents want. At the same time we should not put our public servants in a position where they will be victims of changes of a political party at the government level. This is an important consideration because the public service is an important part of our working environment in Canada. They are dedicated people who work long hours and have long careers. I believe we must take that into consideration as well.
